text: {"score":3,"justification":"Most numbers match the card (9.2%, 2,337, 3.5%, 5.37, 0.88, 20%, 17 docs, 1 of 11). The caution and the flagging of missing 99215 documentation are good. However, the narrative contains a claim the card contradicts, plus some internal inconsistency and loose phrasing, so an investigator would have to redo some checks. The next steps are also generic and do not name specific claims.","problems":["Headline says 99215 is above expectation \"in every complexity tier\", and the rationale says the share runs above the all-provider share in every stratum. The card does show higher shares in every row, but this is compared with the all-provider share, not with an expected share by tier. The wording is looser than the data supports.","The rationale claims that the billing mix \"sits heavily at 99214\" suggests a general upward shift. That is a speculative inference, and it sits oddly beside the 99215 argument.","Contradictory framing: it says the elevated rate is not explained by panel acuity, then says the z-score is unremarkable (0.88) and the records review is too thin to judge. The two are not reconciled, and the weak peer z-score is not explained.","Describes diagnoses as low back pain, upper respiratory infection or a follow-up code for the cited claims. C0122452 (M54.50), C0122494 (M54.50), C0123335 (J06.9) and C0124512 (Z09) are consistent. But it says \"hard to justify\" a top-level visit, which is stronger than the evidence allows without charts.","Text repeats itself (no 99215 documented stated twice; the thin-records point appears several times).","Next steps are generic: no specific claim IDs in the step, and \"re-screen\" is vague. The mention of prioritizing the low-complexity samples is only in the rationale.","Example claim C0122551 (billed 99213, straightforward MDM) is below billed level but is not tied to the 99215 concern, so it adds little for the main issue.","The summary does not explain that 99215 expected share was computed by risk adjustment, nor give excess claims (about 132) which would be a useful number."]}
